state.misconception_label: Struggles to visualise nets of 3D shapes

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This is the net of a... ![A circle touching a sector](). I got Triangle because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have a cardboard box that you need to fold up to form a 3D shape. The net you have drawn is like the unfolded cardboard box, showing all the faces that will come together to create the shape. In this case, the net you drew is for a triangular-based pyramid, not just a triangle. Let's walk through how the faces connect to form the 3D shape.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I get that the net is for a triangular-based pyramid, but I'm still a bit confused. So, the triangle is just one part of it, right? How do the other parts fit together to make the whole shape?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine if you were building a house out of blocks. The triangle you see on the net is like one of the walls of the house. To create the full triangular-based pyramid, you need to add the other walls and the base as well. Just like how all the walls and the base come together to form the complete house, all the faces on the net come together to create the 3D shape. Let's visualize how each face fits together to form the entire triangular-based pyramid.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher provides analogies (cardboard box, house) but never directly addresses the student's visualization struggle or guides them through the actual folding process, and the student's final turn shows they remain confused about how the faces connect, with no evidence of improved reasoning.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete, everyday analogies (unfolding a cardboard box, building a house out of blocks) to help the student understand the abstract concept of nets and 3D shapes, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
